name: uniQure N.V.

profile.description: uniQure N.V. is an AAV gene therapy company that developed HEMGENIX, the hemophilia B gene therapy commercialized by CSL Behring, and is now focused on AMT-130 for Huntington's disease plus AMT-260 (refractory epilepsy) and AMT-191 (Fabry disease) [1][5][8]. After the FDA initially steered AMT-130 toward a lengthy sham-controlled trial, a June 2026 Type B meeting aligned on an accelerated-approval filing; the BLA was announced around September 2, 2026, but four-year data on September 29 triggered a ~37% one-day selloff [2]. The company held $810.3M of cash and investments at June 30, 2026, which it says funds operations into 2030 [1].

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): uniQure brought HEMGENIX to approval as a one-time hemophilia B gene therapy (list price $3.5M), a significant launch that opened a royalty stream it partly monetized for a $375M upfront payment, and has now taken AMT-130 to a US BLA [5][6][2]. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI products, AI-enabled discovery programs or quantified AI savings were found in company materials or coverage [3]. Market Share (1/2): HEMGENIX was first-in-class, but H.C. Wainwright notes CSL's launch has been slower than expected and uniQure only earns royalties, so it is a meaningful participant rather than a share leader [5]. Pipeline (2/2): AMT-130 BLA submitted Q3 2026 with an MHRA filing planned, AMT-260 higher-dose epilepsy data due H1 2027, and AMT-191 Fabry cohorts under evaluation [1][2]. R&D Intensity (1/1): FY2025 R&D of $140.7M was nearly 9x revenue of $16.1M, top-quartile intensity even for biotech [9].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): uniQure states it develops treatments for patients suffering from rare and devastating diseases — clear about what it does and for whom, but not distinctive among gene therapy peers [8][3]. Community Impact (0/2): Research surfaced no foundation, patient-access program or quantified community investment; coverage instead highlighted the $3.5M HEMGENIX price, above ICER's ~$2.9M fair-price ceiling [6]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention data was found; Simply Wall St characterizes the management team as inexperienced with roughly 2 years average tenure, despite a Chief People Officer who says the company measures and acts on culture feedback [4][3]. Insider Buying (0/2): No meaningful net insider buying was identified in the last 12 months.

infrastructure.label: WEAK
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on 6 available growth-sleeve metrics (weighted sum 1.56 of 8; PEG unavailable). Only TTM revenue growth of 11% (license income on ~$18.7M revenue) hits its target, and D/E of 170% earns partial credit (0.56) given $552M of debt against the $810M cash pile [8][1]. Everything else scores zero: ROE of -158%, a FY2025 net margin of roughly -1,236% (net loss of $199M on $16.1M revenue), a negative forward P/E of -8.4, and a 5-year revenue CAGR of -15.6% from FY2020's $37.5M — revenue spiked to $524M in 2021 on the HEMGENIX license and has since collapsed to royalty levels [9][8]. Liquidity is ample at ~$50M of daily dollar volume.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): uniQure's value rests on regulated, clinically validated AAV gene therapies, proprietary manufacturing know-how and patents — physical biologic products that AI cannot substitute, and no analyst coverage found flags AI as a threat [2][5]. It sits below the immune tier because AI-accelerated drug discovery could compress the timelines of competing Huntington's and hemophilia programs, eroding first-mover advantages. AI Opportunity (0/1): The company generates no identifiable AI revenue and has not disclosed AI programs [3].

infinite_game.summary: uniQure has pursued a genuinely hard problem — a one-time therapy for Huntington's disease — for years and has continued after a public FDA reversal, which Sinek would see as a cause worth sacrificing for [2][7]. But its posture is that of a company fighting to survive regulatory binary events: it sold part of its HEMGENIX royalty for cash, faces a securities class action and a reported FDA rebuke over data presentation, and its long-term identity depends on a single program [6][7].

just_cause.analysis: Delivering transformative gene therapies to patients with devastating diseases like Huntington's — a field with no disease-modifying treatment — is a service-oriented cause leadership consistently references, and the company kept investing $140M+ a year in R&D to advance it [8][9]. It has not yet been validated by an approved CNS product or multi-decade consistency (2/3).

trusting_teams.analysis: CEO Matt Kapusta has led the company since December 2016 after joining as CFO in 2015, giving rare leadership continuity for a small biotech [4]. However, the broader management team averages roughly 2 years of tenure and no retention data is published, so trust is adequate rather than exceptional (1/2) [4].

worthy_rivals.analysis: No management commentary was found that frames competitors in Huntington's or hemophilia gene therapy as worthy rivals to learn from; communications focus on regulatory positioning for AMT-130 [1][2]. Insufficient evidence of an infinite competitive mindset (0/1).

existential_flexibility.analysis: uniQure has reshaped its model — licensing HEMGENIX to CSL Behring and selling the lowest royalty tier for $375M to fund a pivot toward CNS diseases like Huntington's and epilepsy [5][6]. These were financing-driven evolutions rather than a cause-driven reinvention (1/2).

courage_to_lead.analysis: Leadership persisted with AMT-130 after the FDA reversal and negotiated a path to accelerated approval while accepting a costly randomized standard-of-care confirmatory study, backed by a follow-on raise that extends runway into 2030 [1][2]. That resolve is offset by a Hagens Berman-reported FDA accusation of 'distorted and manipulated' data presentation, so courage is evident but not a clean pattern (1/2) [7].

investment_thesis: uniQure could own the first disease-modifying therapy for Huntington's disease: AMT-130's BLA was submitted in Q3 2026 after a June Type B meeting aligned on an accelerated-approval path, an MHRA filing is planned, and a widely reported October 28 headline cites FDA acceptance with priority review [1][2]. With $810.3M of cash and investments funding operations into 2030, a HEMGENIX royalty stream, and follow-on shots in epilepsy (AMT-260 data H1 2027) and Fabry disease, the company is financed through a potential launch, and the stock at ~$24.8 sits far below its $51.72 high [1][2].
thesis_continued: The bear case is regulatory and credibility risk: the stock fell ~37% on September 29 after four-year data, the FDA wants a randomized standard-of-care confirmatory study well underway before any accelerated approval, and an advisory committee is expected with no timing guidance [2]. A securities class action follows reports the FDA accused uniQure of presenting 'distorted and manipulated' data, revenue is only ~$18.7M of license income against a FY2025 net loss of $199M, and $552M of debt plus likely dilution weigh on equity holders [7][8][9].
key_catalysts: FDA acceptance/priority review and an eventual PDUFA decision on the AMT-130 BLA for Huntington's disease, plus the planned UK MHRA marketing application [1][2]
Q3 2026 results on November 4 — consensus expects a loss of about $0.84 per share on ~$7.2M revenue, with updates on BLA review timing and advisory committee plans [2]
AMT-260 higher-dose refractory epilepsy data in H1 2027 and clarity on restarting AMT-191 Fabry dose cohorts could diversify value beyond AMT-130 [2]
key_risks: Regulatory: the FDA may require a substantially enrolled randomized confirmatory study or an advisory committee could vote negatively, delaying or denying accelerated approval for AMT-130 [2]
Litigation and credibility: an ongoing securities class action tied to reports that the FDA rebuked uniQure over AMT-130 data presentation [7]
Financial: FY2025 net loss of $199M on $16.1M revenue, $552M of debt and a slower-than-expected HEMGENIX royalty ramp leave the company reliant on capital markets if launch timing slips [5][8][9]
